attack_chains.title: Reversible Credentials → HTTP/HTTPS Admin Access
attack_chains.attack_narrative: Attacker can: 1) decode the Type 7 enable or user passwords from the running config → 2) authenticate to the HTTP or HTTPS management interface (no source IP restriction) → 3) gain full device administrative access (privilege 15).

attack_chains.title: Trunk Native VLAN 1 → VLAN Hopping
attack_chains.attack_narrative: Attacker can: 1) connect to trunk port Gi1/0/4 with native VLAN 1 → 2) send double-tagged frames with outer VLAN 1 and inner VLAN 500 → 3) bypass VLAN segmentation to reach VLAN 500 resources, as evidenced by active MAC learning on the trunk for both VLANs.

attack_chains.title: No Port Security → MAC Flooding & CAM Table Poisoning
attack_chains.attack_narrative: Attacker can: 1) Connect to unprotected access port Gi1/0/6, Gi1/0/7, or Gi1/0/8 in VLAN 500 → 2) Flood switch with spoofed MAC addresses to exhaust CAM table → 3) Force switch into hub-like behavior, flooding traffic to all ports in VLAN 500 → 4) Intercept sensitive traffic or perform man-in-the-middle attacks within VLAN 500.

attack_chains.title: MAC Spoofing → VLAN Hopping Bypass
attack_chains.attack_narrative: Attacker can: 1) spoof MAC addresses observed on trunk port Gi1/0/4 in VLAN 1 (0050.56bf.29d2, 0050.56bf.33e9) → 2) send traffic tagged with VLAN 500 → 3) bypass VLAN access controls by appearing as legitimate VLAN 1 traffic on the trunk, exploiting the absence of port security and VLAN ACLs.

attack_chains.title: VLAN 1 User Traffic → STP Manipulation Risk
attack_chains.attack_narrative: Attacker can: 1) Connect to VLAN 1 via access port Gi1/0/5 (f4-0) → 2) Send malicious BPDUs to trunk port Gi1/0/4 (f5-2) to manipulate Spanning Tree, as global BPDU guard is absent (f1-9) → 3) Force a topology change or become the root bridge, causing a denial of service or traffic redirection, given the switch is currently root for all VLANs (f5-1).

attack_chains.title: Active VLANs → CDP Reconnaissance & Network Mapping
attack_chains.attack_narrative: Attacker can: 1) Use CDP information from any compromised neighbor to learn this switch's hostname, platform, and all connected interfaces → 2) Map the network topology and identify this switch as a central Catalyst 9000 device → 3) Target specific VLANs (1-6, 11, 21, 31, 41, 50, 51, 500) for further attacks based on the expanded VLAN surface.

attack_chains.title: Static MAC on VLAN Interface → ARP Poisoning Anchor
attack_chains.attack_narrative: Attacker can: 1) target the statically mapped MAC address 0050.56bf.2919 on VLAN 1 interface → 2) perform ARP poisoning to impersonate the VLAN 1 gateway → 3) intercept and manipulate all VLAN 1 user traffic flowing through the switch.

outputs.reasoning: We have a priority list: 'show mac address-table vlan 1', 'show mac address-table vlan 500', or 'show spanning-tree detail'. From the running config, we know VLAN 1 is the native VLAN on trunk Gi1/0/4, and we saw dynamic MACs (0050.56bf.29d2, 0050.56bf.33e9) on VLAN 1 via Gi1/0/4. VLAN 500 has three access ports (Gi1/0/6-8) and dynamic MACs on two of them. The attack chain c1-1 (Trunk Native VLAN 1 → VLAN Hopping) is confirmed, but we need to verify if VLAN 1 traffic is actually present (MAC table per VLAN) to assess risk of double-tagging attacks. Also, c4-0 (VLAN 1 User Traffic → STP Manipulation Risk) is likely; checking MACs on VLAN 1 will confirm if there is active user traffic in VLAN 1 that could be leveraged for STP attacks. 'show mac address-table vlan 1' will confirm the presence of active hosts in the native VLAN, which compounds with the native VLAN misconfiguration to strengthen the VLAN hopping chain.
